So, I realized you can take the person out of the ghetto, but you can't take the ghetto out of the person. The ghetto is inside them. It's part of them. They'll take it with them wherever they go.

I had a friend who developed a crack problem, but her distant dad just thought he could solve her problems by throwing money at her. He bought her a brand new, 4 bedroom, pretty nice house, but it was in a bad neighborhood and she was still a crack addict. She was a beautiful, young, talented girl except for the crack. After the first week, there were holes in the wall and animal feces all over the floor with 8 newborn puppies. People would party there all the time and it got covered in graffiti. They started cooking it in her kitchen, and her house ended up becoming a crack house. So again it's not all ghetto people, but there are certainly plenty who will literally take the ghetto with them. And you see the results of that when you take a random sample of them and try to put them in an upgraded environment. It does not bring them up, instead, they bring it down to their level. This is why you see phenomenon like fast degradation and the subsequent middle class flight from areas that try to help by importing them into their own nicer environments.

I think your mistake is that you see these people as victims of their environment, and you abdicate that they should take any responsibility for themselves. But actually, they are responsible for themselves and they do influence their environment, very much so, in fact. Sure, you could save some of them (especially younger kids), but you can't save their parents, you can't save the drug addicts, and you can't save most of them from their own choices.

It's like the girl I mentioned, her rich dad thought he could just throw money at the problem and that would solve it. But he completely ignored the root cause, the deep underlying issue, and the results speak for themselves. Money just can't solve these kinds of problems. And it's not just the druggies, they're more of a symptom then a cause. It's a general culture that creates and supports trashiness and violence. That culture doesn't just disappear when you improve the infrastructure around it with money. And that money? It's not going to go to creative entrepreneurship and innovation and creating a new culture. It's going to be invested within that culture, and probably exacerbate it.

That's a bit of a false dichotomy. Personal accountability and victim of circumstance are not mutually exclusive. Like many social issues, I think the truth is probably somewhere in between. As for culture problems, I completely agree although I think that gets incredibly tangential. Think about the change in the American business culture as well. Things are getting pretty bad, culturally, on the top and bottom.

There's one thing that I think most of your anecdotes here miss out on though. Your anecdotes are all about covering some need or another. Basic income isn't a rationing or housing program or anything of the sort. It is 100% up to people what they choose to do with that money. It ought be enough to provide a bare minimum living, but if somebody wants to go spend it all on #13 at the roulette table - he certainly can. What basic income offers is freedom. What people do with that freedom is up to them.

That in my opinion is a big part of why all these voucher programs and the like are mostly just colossal wastes of money. I had a big brother as part of the Big Brothers Big Sisters of America program from United Way - a man who's still like a brother to me. And I think that was incredibly beneficial. When considering college I was able to fly around the country and even had the means to be able to spend a week on campus at MIT. I also got to see and experience so much more. I never really realized what he was doing. But in hindsight the entertainment, food, and everything we ever did was all constantly geared towards things I'd never have experienced before - and I hadn't. A poor kid from the south going to downtown musicals, rock climbing, eating at Brazilian steakhouses, and going on a casual boating trip around the Aleutians? I now live half way around the world working on getting my own business going. In hindsight, none of this would have ever happened without the freedom I was fortunate enough to have had (and been exposed to) in my early life.

Basic income would begin to enable freedom. Our entire system is not about freedom, but about exactly what you're talking about - rationing and allocating. You need a house, here's a voucher for a house. You need some food, here's a voucher for food. Freedom - the responsibility, the possibility, the options - that is what I think life is really about.

And finally we get to automation. I think the reasons that McDonalds is not more actively pursuing automation have very little to do with the capability for it. A bigger issue is public relations. That's a lie of course, but the reason they're forced to play these games is because there's already a backlash against corporate greed. I'm currently in England and we just got those things last year. I love them. Hahah, I think we finally agree on something! I agree with just about everything here except your view of automation. Automation will not just be replacing low skilled jobs. Arguably the first job to be taken over by modern automation has already happened - the employed stock trader. There still are some, but that industry has been mostly taken over by automated systems. There was a great article a long time back (I want to say 2004) about the rise of enhanced productivity tools being used by large firms. Problem is the tools, which were built to just aid the traders, started becoming more effective than the traders - and the traders became obsolete. Zoom forward to today and 84% of trades in the market are created by AIs. To be clear this doesn't mean you setting a sell-at price for your stocks, but rather unique trades and trading strategies created and autonomously carried out by automated systems. There's also some cool work being done on automating surgery, and legal work is already being automated as well major potential for exponentially increasing the automation of the entire legal industry.

That said, there is a constant balance here. The sort of marketing speak here is pretty typical:

The fast-food chain denies [the kiosks are designed to replace humans.] McDonald's spokeswoman Lisa McComb says cashiers will still be taking orders.

"Similar to ordering from an app, the technology (any technology such as self-order kiosk, mobile phone, web ordering), offers additional service options, giving customers the ability to control the way they wish to experience and engage with McDonald’s," McComb told Business Insider.

Fascinating stuff really, I'm still trying to get over the internet existing, and now all this automation. It's really amazing if you step back and look at how fast humans are progressing.
